title: Choosing Between Voice, Text, and Neither
text: Hi, I'm Harshita Nimble, a product designer. Here's today's ask. The same AI feature, a voice assistant, a coding tool, whatever, sometimes talks to you, sometimes waits for you to type, and sometimes says nothing at all. What decides which one is right? AI's best input isn't voice, it's whichever fits the moment. Hands busy, talk to it. Need exact words or privacy, type to it.

title: Voice Input: Hands and Eyes Busy
text: Sometimes say nothing and let it act. Start with voice. Google's Assistant driving mode launches with "Hey Google, let's drive." and hands every task, texts, calls, music to voice alone, hands never leaving the wheel. That's not a stylistic choice. It's the only input that works when your eyes and hands are already busy driving. Now, the opposite context, an open office writing code. GitHub Copilot suggests code

title: Text Input: Exact Wording and Privacy
text: Inline as dimmed text, never spoken aloud, nothing runs or saves until you press tab. Typing keeps exact syntax exact and keeps your prompts private from the desk next to you. Voice would be slower here and a lot more awkward. Line those up in a pattern shows, three input modes, three different jobs. Voice, when hands or eyes are busy.

title: The "Neither" Mode: Invisible Automation (Gmail, Nest)
text: Text, when wording must be exact or private. And a third option almost nobody designs on purpose. Neither, the AI just acts and nobody has to say a word. That third mode is easy to miss because it's invisible by design. Gmail's spam filter blocks more than 99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, billions of emails a day, without you ever typing a search or saying a command. You only notice it on the rare day it's wrong. Same idea in your house. The Nest

title: The Cost of "Neither" and the 3 Decision Questions
text: Learning thermostat watches what temperature you actually choose, at what times, for about a week, then builds its own schedule. No app to configure, no voice command. You just live your life and it quietly learns the pattern. Here's why matching the mode matters. The wrong input adds a tax every single time. Fumbling to type while driving is dangerous. Speaking a private query out loud is embarrassing. And asking permission for something trivial is just annoying. Match the mode and that tax disappears. Line up the mismatch against the match. Voice in a quiet office is disruptive. Voice when your hands are busy is right. Typing while driving is dangerous. Typing when precision or privacy matters is right. Acting without asking on something big is unsettling. On something small and reversible, it's exactly right. Same three modes, completely different fit. The neither mode has a real cost. It usually means always listening. And always listening can

Go wrong. Apple agreed to pay $95 million to dollars to settle a lawsuit after Siri was found to record private conversations by accident, medical details, business calls, without anyone asking it to. So, before you default to a chat box or a voice assistant, ask three questions. Are the user's hands or eyes busy? Does the wording need to be exact or private? And is this small and reversible enough to skip asking entirely? The answer picks the input for you. Your turn. Pick one AI feature you use and ask Claude. Are your hands or eyes usually busy when you use it? Does the wording need to be exact or private? Or is the action small and reversible enough to need no input at all? Then ask whether it's actually using the right mode today or just the one it's designers defaulted to. Voice, text, or neither. Designing the right input for AI. I'm Harshada Nimble.
